newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIA BOND YIELDS EDGE UP, BUT SEEN SHORTLIVED.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIA BOND YIELDS EDGE UP, BUT SEEN SHORTLIVED.

text.p: *Australian bond yields edged up after the July labour force report contained a surprise 52,500 jump in full-time employment, although the overall 21,300 increase was roughly as expected.
*Data not seen changing opinions over policy outlook.
Australian bond yields crept above their early lows after the July labour force report contained a surprise 52,500 jump in full-time employment.

However, the overall employment outcome was a shade below median expectations, and analysts pointed out that the full/part-time split is constantly volatile, which should make the mildly negative reaction short-lived.

"The market had got very bullish before the data, and just seeing the full-time bounce just took a little bit of edge off what is still a faily weak number," said Stephen Roberts, chief economist at UBS Australia.

Overall employment rose 21,300, well short of 60,000-plus that was needed to put employment growth on a firmer footing, while the unemployment rate rose to 8.7 percent from 8.5 percent and just above the median 8.6 percent expected.

"The unemployment rate is really stuck above 8.5 percent and we don't see that coming down in a hurry. It certainly puts pressure on some policy response either from fiscal or monetary policy." said Nigel Douglas, chief economist at Merrill Lynch Australia.
However, the analysts felt the data was unlikely to change people's views over the monetary policy outlook.
A Reuters poll of economists taken last Friday gave a 30 percent chance of another rate cut after last week's 1/2 point easing to 5.0 percent by the Reserve Bank.

Bill futures also eased back from their initial highs on the employment report, although the September position at 95.10 still equates to a cash rate of 4.90 percent, suggesting the market has not completely given up on a further easing.
The focus now switches back to the U.S. Treasury market which faces the final leg of the quarterly refunding auctions with the offer US$10 billion of 30-year bonds later on Thursday.

The local market's minor pull back saw spreads to the U.S. and Canada reverse their initial tightening. However, the negative spread to New Zealand continued to grow as the N.Z. currency remained vulberable and after its NZ$150 million tender of July 2009 bonds.
